meanings.note: Points to the speaker's location or reinforces demonstratives like isso aqui and esse slide aqui.

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: Used casually for a workplace motto or guiding principle.

examples.text: Aqui a gente tem uma filosofia.
Essa é a filosofia da empresa.

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

poder.gloss: can; may; to be able to

meanings.en: can; may; to be able to
meanings.note: Core modal verb followed by an infinitive.

examples.text: O senhor pode ser meu fiador?
examples.trans: Can you be my guarantor, sir?

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.
Regular -er verb in present and past (morreu); irregular participle morto.
Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Stronger and warmer than bonito.

examples.text: Vimos uma paisagem linda na estrada.
examples.trans: We saw a gorgeous landscape on the road.

meanings.note: Connects a conclusion or agreement.
In harmonização facial, a popular Brazilian cosmetic filler package.

examples.text: A harmonização facial dá uma bela rejuvenescida.
examples.trans: Facial harmonization gives a lovely rejuvenation.

meanings.note: Relating to the face, as in harmonização facial.

examples.trans: The facial harmonization turned out great.

meanings.note: Versatile core verb; dando falsa esperança means giving false hope.

examples.text: Ele está dando falsa esperança pra nós.
examples.trans: He is giving us false hope.

meanings.note: Before an action noun in dar uma bela rejuvenescida, means 'a really nice/proper'.

examples.trans: It gives a lovely rejuvenation, right?

meanings.note: In dar uma rejuvenescida, a colloquial Brazilian construction turning a participle into a quick action noun.

examples.trans: It gives a lovely rejuvenation, right?
The haircut gave a fresh, younger look.

meanings.note: Ubiquitous spoken contraction of não é used to invite agreement.

examples.text: Isso aqui é um gráfico, né?
examples.trans: This here is a chart, right?

meanings.note: Interrogative pronoun for people.
Informal singular object pronoun, routinely mixed with você in warm everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

meanings.note: Takes a before an infinitive: autorizou a fazer.

examples.text: Quem que te autorizou a fazer isso?
examples.trans: Who authorized you to do this?

meanings.note: Links verbs like faltar to an event or destination.
Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Vamos seguir moves a meeting along to the next topic or slide.

examples.trans: We have to look into it. Let's move on.

meanings.note: Special fused form of com + mim; Portuguese says gritar comigo where English says shout at me.

examples.trans: Did you need to shout at me?
Come to the meeting with me.

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.
In no caso de, means in the case of.

examples.text: No caso da sua mãe, foi diferente.
examples.trans: In the case of your mother, it was different.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Possessive determiner agreeing with the possessed noun; in Brazil it most often means your (with você).

examples.text: É isso que você quer pra sua vida?
examples.trans: Is that what you want for your life?

meanings.note: Female parent; plural mães.

examples.text: Meu pai e minha mãe me bloquearam.
examples.trans: My dad and my mom blocked me.

examples.text: Vou voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Third-person feminine singular pronoun; in informal Brazilian speech olha pra ela uses ela after a preposition too.
A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Back grinding tooth.

examples.text: Ela não tinha os molares ali do fundo.
examples.trans: She did not have those back molars there.

meanings.note: Points to something visible a short distance away.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?
The room is right over there.

meanings.note: Used adverbially in respirar fundo (to breathe deeply).

examples.text: Abraça o corpo e respira fundo.
examples.trans: Cross your arms and breathe deeply.

examples.text: Ele respirou fundo antes de falar.
examples.trans: He took a deep breath before speaking.

meanings.note: Used in O que está acontecendo? (What is going on?) and O que aconteceu foi que... (What happened was that...).
Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
The jaw area in dental and aesthetic speech.

examples.text: O maxilar dela ficou bem caidinho.
examples.trans: Her jaw ended up quite droopy.
He feels pain in his jaw.

meanings.note: Contraction of de + ela, placed after the noun in Brazil to mean her.

examples.trans: She got ahead on her work.

meanings.note: Expresses staying in a place or state (ficar sentado, fica no celular).

examples.text: Ela fica no celular o dia todo.
examples.trans: She stays on her phone all day.

meanings.note: Modifies a verb to mean well or carefully, as in olhar bem (look closely).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Diminutive of caído (fallen/droopy), softening the critique.

examples.text: O maxilar dela ficou bem caidinho.
examples.trans: Her jaw ended up quite droopy.

examples.text: O olho ficou um pouco caidinho.
examples.trans: The eye looked a bit droopy.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
English cosmetic loanword used in Brazilian clinics for a facelift.

examples.text: Eu fiz o lifting no rosto.
examples.trans: I did the facelift on her face.

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Used with para/pra for going back to a place.

examples.text: Vou ter que voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to have to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Contraction of de + aqui.

examples.text: A dor pega daqui até o pescoço.
examples.trans: The pain goes from here up to my neck.

meanings.note: Invariable cardinal number.

examples.trans: I will deposit up to six months.

meanings.note: Calendar month; plural meses drops the circumflex.

examples.trans: I will deposit up to six months.

examples.text: Falta um mês para a viagem.
examples.trans: There is one month left until the trip.

meanings.note: Points to manner or way.

examples.text: A gente não gosta de ser chamada assim.
examples.trans: We do not like to be called that.

meanings.note: Often reinforced with é que in questions (como é que foi?).

examples.text: Como é que foi a cirurgia?
Como é que tá meu marido?

meanings.note: Marks comparisons (mais que), negated continuation (não ... mais, not anymore), and the farewell até mais.
